%%
%% The abstract is a short summary of the work to be presented in the
%% article.
\begin{abstract}
Understanding how online communities accommodate moral disagreement requires looking beyond their final verdicts to how they respond to challenges to collective blame and collective defense. We distinguish blaming dissent, which assigns fault to someone most others defend, from defending dissent, which rejects fault assigned by most others. Focusing on r/AmItheAsshole (AITA), with an extension to r/AITAH (AITAH), we analyze more than 15 million top-level judgment comments, combining scores and reply structure with annotations of direct responses and expressed linguistic certainty. Our primary focus is high-agreement posts, where at least 80\% of judgments favor one side; low-agreement posts provide a comparison. We first revisit the established pattern of lower scores but greater reply engagement for minority comments and find that it recurs in both directions of dissent. Beyond this shared pattern, blaming dissent receives lower mean scores and attracts more replies and deeper reply trees than defending dissent. Annotated replies from other commenters also show higher challenge rates toward minority than majority judgments across the analyzed strata. Separating blaming from defending also reveals differences in expressed certainty. In high-agreement AITA posts, blaming dissent has modestly higher post-averaged certainty over the full observed period and a higher proportion of certainty-4 comments than defending dissent; the low-agreement contrast remains uncertain. The AITAH extension yields positive directional point estimates, but small cohorts limit their interpretation. These aggregate contrasts do not establish temporal convergence, silence, or individual attitude change. Together, the findings show why assessing a community's response to moral disagreement requires distinguishing which judgments its minority voices challenge, rather than treating all dissent as equivalent.
\end{abstract}
